title: Reverse Pairs
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums`. Call a pair of indices `(i, j)` a *reverse pair* when `i < j` and the earlier value is strictly more than double the later one, that is `nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]`. Return how many reverse pairs the array contains.

The values span the full 32-bit signed range, so `2 * nums[j]` may not fit in a 32-bit integer.
notes:
## Intuition

Testing every pair is O(n²), far too slow for 5 * 10^4 values. Merge sort helps: when the left half and the right half of a range are each sorted, the pairs that cross the middle can be counted with one forward-moving pointer, because a larger left value can only beat *more* right values, never fewer. Pairs that stay inside one half were already counted by the recursive calls, and sorting a half never changes which side of the middle a value sits on.

## Approach

1. Copy `nums` into `sorted` and make a scratch array `buffer` for merging.
2. `countPairs(low, high)` handles the half-open range `[low, high)`; a range of 0 or 1 values has no pairs.
3. Split at `mid`, and add the counts of both halves (each call also sorts its half).
4. With `j` starting at `mid`, walk `i` through the sorted left half. Advance `j` while `sorted[i] > 2 * sorted[j]`; then `j - mid` right values pair with `sorted[i]`. `j` never moves back, because the next `sorted[i]` is at least as big.
5. Merge the two sorted halves through `buffer` and copy them back, so the caller sees a sorted range.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 3, 2, 3, 1]`, `mid = 2`. The left half `[1, 3]` has no pairs and becomes `[1, 3]`. The right half `[2, 3, 1]` splits into `[2]` and `[3, 1]`; inside `[3, 1]`, `3 > 2 * 1` gives `count = 1`, and it sorts to `[1, 3]`. `2 > 2 * 1` fails, so the right half reports 1 and becomes `[1, 2, 3]`. At the top, `i` reads `1` (no right value qualifies, `j` stays at `mid`) and then `3` (`3 > 2 * 1`, so `j` moves once and adds 1). The answer is `0 + 1 + 1 = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): each of the log n levels does a linear counting pass and a linear merge.
- Space: O(n) for `sorted` and `buffer`, plus O(log n) recursion depth.

## Pitfalls

- `2 * nums[j]` overflows a 32-bit `int` (try `-2147483648`); in Java or C compute it as a 64-bit value.
- Count before merging: once the halves are merged you no longer know which value came from which side.
- The test is strict: `nums[i] = 2 * nums[j]` is not a reverse pair.
- Do not reset `j` for each `i`, or the counting pass becomes quadratic.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sorted` | copy of `nums` that each call sorts within its range |
| `buffer` | scratch space used while merging |
| `low`, `high` | the half-open range `[low, high)` being handled |
| `mid` | first index of the right half |
| `count` | reverse pairs found inside `[low, high)` |
| `i`, `j` | pointers into the left and right halves while counting |
| `left`, `right`, `k` | read positions in each half and write position in `buffer` while merging |
| `t` | index used to copy the merged range back |
